drills.coachNote: White's king on f4 has nowhere to run — your rook on e3, rook on e8, and bishop on h3 already cover every flight square, so this is mate-in-one, not just check. R3e4+ only checks: it lets the king slide to g3, and because your e3 rook just left, nothing guards your bishop on h3 anymore — White grabs it with Kxh3, turning a forced mate into merely a big material edge. The actual finish is g5#: the pawn covers f4's escape squares while your rook and bishop seal the rest. When you spot a mating net, don't settle for a check — check whether it's already checkmate.

drills.coachNote: White's king on f4 is stuck in a mating net built from your rook on e3, rook on e8, and bishop on h3 — the point is to keep it in check, not to pause. Bxg2 grabs a pawn but isn't check, so White gets a free move, Ra6, to start untangling, and your bishop later gets harassed by Kg3 while the attack loses its bite — that pause costs you about 13 pawns of advantage. The engine's g5+ keeps the king running: Kf5 Rf2+ Kg4 Rxg2+ Kf5 wins the same pawn but never lets White breathe. In a king hunt, keep the checks coming before you shop for material.

drills.coachNote: The whole difference between winning cleanly and grinding it out here is the f4 square — if you control it, White's f3 pawn can never break free and open lines for his king. Kd4 doesn't touch f4 (it's two files away), so White plays f4! and after gxf4 Kc2 his king dashes into the game, complicating what should be simple and costing you roughly 9 pawns of winning margin. Ke5 does the job instead: it guards f4 outright, and after Kc2 Kf4 Kd3 a5 your king marches in while White's king stays stuck. In king endings, station your king to kill the opponent's only pawn break before marching anywhere else.
drills.threat: Whoever controls the f4 square decides if White's f3 pawn can break free — right now nothing of yours guards it.
